newsitem.title: KENYA: Serena issue opens at Nairobi bourse.
newsitem.headline: Serena issue opens at Nairobi bourse.

text.p: The initial public offering on the Nairobi Stock Exchange of shares in Serena Hotels opened on Monday and will close on April 14, brokers said.
Serena Hotels is the trading name of Serena Lodges & Hotels. Shares offered for sale belong to the majority Aga Khan-owned Tourism Promotion Services, which operates the Serena Hotels.
Brokers said the sale of a total 9,025,100 shares at an initial price of 13 to the public would be oversubcribed.
"The shares on offer are too few and will not quench the public's thirst for new issues," a senior broker said.

At 13, the shares are discounted from the net asset value per share price of 13.63 given in the prospectus on the basis of their audited accounts for the year ended December 31, 1996, according to market analysts.
"The price is a Kenyan price. Many Kenyans fear anything above 50, and it should not be difficult to raise the capital (Serena envisages)," another broker said.
The offer for sale represents a 23.3 percent holding in Tourism Promotion Services held by government tourism agency Kenya Tourism Development Corporation (KTDC).
The government says by pulling out of Serena, it will give mostly ordinary Kenyans a chance to invest in one of the East African country's leading luxury hotels.
The KTDC holds a 33.3 percent stake in Tourism Promotion Services. It will retain a 10 percent holding.
Market analysts forecast a scramble for what they described as scarce shares and saw attention mainly from investors who sought a chance to diversify their portfolio.

"The tourism industry, one of Kenya's biggest foreign exchange earners, is underepresented in the market," a broker said. "With a 60 percent occupancy, Serena has growth potential and investors will benefit from profitability of the industry."
The only other hotel concern listed on the Nairobi Stock Exchange is African Tours & Hotels.
Serena falls in the high premium segment of the tourism industry which was least affected by declining inflows of tourists to Kenya in recent years, market experts said.
The offer is open to foreigners, subject to rules that restrict such investment to 40 percent in a company and five percent for every individual in one company.
